nodes.title: Lessons from Mt. Stupid (the fabricated curve)
nodes.claim: Blog post that paired the Dunning-Kruger name with a peak-and-trough 'Mt. Stupid' curve that appears in no Dunning-Kruger paper.
nodes.note: Earliest known version of the viral curve; the chart, not the studies, is what the culture now cites.

nodes.title: Dunning-Kruger effect (Wikipedia)
nodes.claim: Defines the effect as poor performers' inability to recognize their own incompetence; covers the 1999 study and the later statistical-artifact critiques.
nodes.note: The amplifier: codified the pop-law reading for millions while quietly hosting the critiques.

nodes.title: The Dunning-Kruger Effect: What It Is & Why It Matters
nodes.claim: Mainstream explainer asserting the effect shows incompetent people overestimating their ability; attributes the finding to the 1999 Kruger-Dunning Cornell studies.
nodes.note: Typical SEO health-media echo that converts ~350 undergrads into universal life advice.

nodes.title: Why incompetent people think they're amazing (TED-Ed)
nodes.claim: Animated lesson in which David Dunning himself presents the effect as people frequently overestimating their own abilities.
nodes.note: The origin author laundered the pop version into edutainment for millions of viewers.

nodes.title: The Dunning-Kruger Effect, Explained (Open Culture)
nodes.claim: Pop explainer of the effect that cites no source paper and omits the statistical-artifact critiques entirely.
nodes.note: Shows the mutation in 2024: the 'law' survives with no paper attached.

nodes.title: Unskilled and unaware of it
nodes.claim: Four small studies of ~350 Cornell undergrads: bottom-quartile performers (~12th percentile) self-estimated near the 62nd percentile.
nodes.note: Origin source; its own authors conceded regression to the mean 'virtually guarantees' the pattern and argued only that it was 'more psychological than artifactual.'

nodes.title: Unskilled, unaware, or both?
nodes.claim: Reanalysis showing the apparent miscalibration of low scorers is produced by regression to the mean plus a better-than-average bias, not a metacognitive deficit.
nodes.note: The 2002 kill-shot the pop version of the effect never mentions.

nodes.title: The Dunning-Kruger effect is (mostly) a statistical artefact
nodes.claim: Using a validated signal-detection method in 929 participants, the apparent Dunning-Kruger effect shrinks to '(mostly) a statistical artefact' of measurement conventions.
nodes.note: Largest-sample methodological verdict; cited by the field, ignored by pop media.

nodes.title: A rational model of the Dunning-Kruger effect
nodes.authors: Jansen RA et al. (Nat Hum Behav)
nodes.claim: A computational model plus two studies of roughly 4,000 people finds low performers are less able to tell whether they are correct, reviving a modest genuine metacognitive deficit.
nodes.note: The honest nuance node: not artifact-only, but a far weaker effect than the meme.

nodes.title: The Dunning-Kruger effect and its discontents
nodes.claim: David Dunning defends the effect as a real metacognitive deficit, arguing the artifact critiques misread the data and ignore contrary research.
nodes.note: Even the origin author now defends only a weakened, qualified version.

nodes.title: Random Number Simulations Reveal How Random Noise Affects Self-Assessed Competency
nodes.claim: Random-number data containing no psychology at all, plotted with the field's quartile conventions, reproduce the classic Dunning-Kruger curve exactly.
nodes.note: The killer counter-truth: the curve is an artifact of plotting; essentially nobody cites it.
